blurb: A low spreading carpet of narrow green leaves opening lemon-yellow four-petalled cups one at a time, all summer. The spent flowers age to orange, so a clump carries both colours at once. It likes heat and lean ground.
water: Low; xeric — well-drained ground, little or no supplemental water once established
spread: Mat-forming: spreading stems knit into a low carpet
seasons: Lemon-yellow four-petalled cups through summer, spent flowers ageing orange; low spreading foliage
wildlife: Native bees and butterflies work the flowers

care.hardiness: CSU lists this as a Colorado native plantable to about 7,000 ft, so cold is not the constraint at Boulder's zone 5b–6a.[1]
care.planting: Plant in spring after the mid-May last frost, or in early fall, into ground prepared to suit it (see Soil). Set out young container plants — most of these natives resent having an established root system disturbed — and water them in well, then taper off.[1][2]
care.sun: Full sun, which is CSU's exposure rating for it.[1]
care.soil: Well-drained soil, and lean. Both *Calylophus* on CSU's list want sharp drainage and heat; rich, damp ground rots the crown.[1]
care.water: Low. CSU rates its moisture requirement low, and on the semi-arid Front Range that is the number that matters most — the commonest way to kill a xeric native here is kindness with the hose.[1][2]
care.spacing: Space to suit its mature spread of spreading. A spreading habit with narrow green leaves and four-petalled flowers borne singly on the stems — CSU notes it is long blooming and likes heat.[1]
care.propagation: By seed, which is how nearly all of these natives are raised and how they persist in a planting. Autumn sowing outdoors lets winter provide the chilling most of them want.[1]
care.bloom: Flowers roughly June through mid-August; CSU records the colour as yellow, orange and the height as 4–8 in tall.[1]
care.maintenance: Low. Cut old growth back in late winter or early spring rather than in fall, so the stems hold snow and give the crown some cover. Skip fertilizer: lean soil keeps these natives compact and long-lived.[1][2]
care.troubles: Few pests or diseases when it is sited right. Crown and root rot in soil that stays wet is the usual cause of failure for a Colorado native in a Front Range garden, and it is a siting problem rather than bad luck.[1][2]

edible.summary: No documented culinary use; grown as a xeric groundcover.[1]
edible.caution: No authority consulted documents a food use for this plant, so this guide treats it as inedible — don't eat it. It sits in the evening-primrose family, some of whose members have a food record, but that does not transfer to this species and this guide does not extend it.[1]
